title: Building better digital twins
gist: A Santa Fe Institute working group (Sept 28-30) on digital twins reports accelerating interest across engineering, disaster response and especially medicine, driven by AI and US agency funding. Open problems are computational demands, siloed multi-scale data, and trust, explainability and validation.

insights.claim: Digital twins, which evolve alongside real-world counterparts through ongoing physical-virtual interaction rather than static snapshots, are being applied from bridges and space shuttles to forest fires, tumors and entire cities.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Defines a broad addressable domain for simulation tooling across infrastructure, aerospace, health and urban management.

insights.claim: Interest in digital twins has surged because advances in AI coincide with growing attention from the NIH, NSF and Department of Defense, which Karen Willcox says is bringing many developments together at once.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Federal research funding and AI progress are tailwinds for digital-twin R&D and related vendors.
insights.quote: There's been an incredible surge of interest in digital twins, and a lot has changed with AI

insights.claim: Medicine shows a particular groundswell of digital-twin interest, but representing a body requires modeling from the genomic level up, incorporating DNA, RNA, metabolism, immune system and lifestyle data.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Data integration across biological scales is the main barrier and the likely value-capture point in health digital twins.
insights.locator: Medicine has seen a particular groundswell

insights.claim: Digital twins could improve on clinical trials, which typically compare one regimen to standard of care, by predicting who will respond better to more or less drug and at more or less frequent dosing intervals.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Personalized dosing simulation could change trial design and precision-oncology economics; watch for adoption in oncology.
insights.quote: The future of cancer includes the right measures, and right interventions, for the right person, at the right time

insights.claim: Complex digital twins must combine several data types across scales, yet groups working on each scale operate in silos, and accuracy suffers from missing data, inconsistent data collection and meaning, and the fast pace of new research findings.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Data standardization and cross-disciplinary integration are bottlenecks; interoperability tooling is a potential opportunity.
insights.quote: Groups working on each scale are working in silos

insights.claim: Open questions for digital twins include managing computational demands, gaining public trust, and deciding how much model detail is needed to improve lives; Willcox says trustworthiness, explainability and validatability will determine adoption.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Trust and validation, not just capability, gate commercial and regulatory uptake.
insights.quote: These issues will make all the difference in their adoption.
insights.locator: How can we make digital twins trustworthy

insights.claim: Working-group co-organizers Karen Willcox, Omar Ghattas and Bart van Bloemen Waanders are developing an edited volume with tutorials and cutting-edge applications to give students and researchers a foundation in digital twin methods.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Signals the field is maturing toward standard methods and training pipelines.
insights.locator: Willcox and the other working group co-organizers
